note: Original practice questions written for Patch Notes. They are not real exam questions.

questions.stem: A colleague says a fault is 'at layer 3'. Which device works at that layer?

options.why: Routers forward packets between networks using IP addresses, which is layer 3 (network).
A standard switch forwards frames using MAC addresses at layer 2 (data link).
A hub just repeats electrical signals out of every port, which is layer 1 (physical).
Browsers work at layer 7 (application).

questions.stem: Which OSI layer adds the source and destination port numbers?

options.why: TCP and UDP add port numbers to segments or datagrams at layer 4.
Layer 3 adds IP addresses, not ports.
Layer 2 adds MAC addresses when it builds the frame.
Layer 5 sets up and manages sessions; it doesn't add port numbers.

questions.stem: Which device spreads incoming web traffic across several servers so no single one is overwhelmed?

options.why: A load balancer shares requests between servers and can stop sending to one that fails.
A proxy makes requests on behalf of clients, often to filter or cache them.
An intrusion detection system watches traffic and raises alerts; it doesn't distribute it.
Network-attached storage serves files over the network.

questions.stem: What's the key difference between an IDS and an IPS?

options.text: An IPS sits in the traffic path and can block it; an IDS only detects and alerts
options.why: Because it's inline, an IPS can drop malicious traffic. An IDS watches a copy and alerts.

options.text: An IDS blocks traffic; an IPS only logs it
options.why: That's the wrong way round.

options.text: An IDS is for wireless networks and an IPS for wired
options.why: Both work on any network; the difference is whether they can block.
The P (prevention) means it can act, not just watch.

questions.stem: A company rents virtual servers from a provider and installs its own operating systems and apps. Which cloud model is this?

options.why: Infrastructure as a service: the provider runs the hardware and virtualisation; you manage everything from the OS up.
With platform as a service the provider also manages the OS and runtime; you just deploy code.
Software as a service is finished software you simply use, such as webmail.
On-premises means you own and run the hardware yourself, so it isn't cloud.

questions.stem: What does a virtual private cloud (VPC) give you?

options.text: A logically isolated private network inside a public cloud
options.why: A VPC is your own network space in the provider's cloud, with your own subnets, routing and firewall rules.

options.text: A physical server you own in the provider's data centre
options.why: That describes a dedicated host or colocation, not a VPC.

options.text: A VPN client for remote staff
options.why: A VPN client connects users; a VPC is the network itself.
Backups are a separate service.

questions.stem: Which TWO protocols send everything, including passwords, unencrypted? (Choose two.)

options.why: Telnet sends the whole session in plain text. Replace it with SSH (port 22).
FTP logins and data cross the network in plain text. Use SFTP or FTPS instead.
SSH encrypts the session.
HTTPS encrypts web traffic with TLS.

questions.stem: A firewall must allow normal DNS lookups. What is mainly needed?

options.why: Most DNS queries use UDP 53. TCP 53 is used for large answers and zone transfers.
Allowing only TCP would break most everyday lookups, which use UDP.
Those are DHCP.
That's NTP, for time.

questions.stem: Which traffic type sends one packet to every device on the local network?

options.why: A broadcast goes to every device in the broadcast domain, e.g. a DHCP Discover.
Unicast is one sender to one receiver.
Multicast reaches only devices that have joined a group.
Anycast delivers to the nearest of several devices sharing one address.

questions.stem: Which cabling is immune to electromagnetic interference and suits long runs between buildings?

options.why: Fibre carries light, not electricity, so EMI can't affect it, and it covers far longer distances.
Copper UTP is affected by interference and is limited to about 100 m.
Coax is shielded copper, so it resists but isn't immune to interference.
Shielding reduces interference but doesn't eliminate it, and the 100 m limit still applies.

questions.stem: What's the maximum recommended length of a twisted-pair Ethernet run, such as Cat 6, from switch to device?

options.why: Twisted-pair Ethernet is specified to 100 m, including patch cables.
Far shorter than the standard allows.
That was an old thick-coax standard, not twisted pair.
Distances like that need fibre.

questions.stem: In a spine-and-leaf data centre network, how is each leaf switch connected?

options.why: Each leaf links to every spine, so any two servers are the same short distance apart and one spine can fail safely.
That would make each spine a single point of failure for its leaves.

options.text: To the other leaf switches in a ring
options.why: Leaves don't connect to each other in spine-and-leaf.
Internet links come in through border devices, not every leaf.

questions.stem: Which topology has no single point of failure because every node connects to every other node?

options.why: With every node linked to every other, traffic can always take another path.
The central switch is a single point of failure.
A break in the shared backbone takes everyone down.
If the hub fails, the spokes can't reach each other.

questions.stem: A PC's address is 169.254.33.10. What does that tell you?

options.text: It couldn't reach a DHCP server, so it gave itself an APIPA address
options.why: 169.254.0.0/16 addresses are self-assigned when DHCP fails. Check the DHCP server and the path to it.

options.text: It has a public internet address
options.why: 169.254 addresses are link-local and never routed.
Possible but unlikely: this range is what Windows picks for itself when DHCP fails.
Loopback is 127.0.0.0/8.

questions.stem: How many usable host addresses does a /27 subnet provide?

options.why: /27 leaves 5 host bits: 2^5 = 32 addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses = 30.
That's the total, including the network and broadcast addresses, which hosts can't use.
That's a /26.
That's a /28.

questions.stem: Which of these is a private (RFC 1918) address?

options.why: 172.32 is just outside the private 172.16–172.31 range, so it's public.
Only 192.168.x.x is private; 192.169 is public.
Only 10.x.x.x is private in that area; 11 is public.

questions.stem: What does SD-WAN mainly do?

options.text: Uses software to choose the best path across several WAN links, such as broadband, 5G and MPLS
options.why: SD-WAN steers each application over whichever link suits it best and fails over automatically.
SD-WAN is about links between sites, not wireless.
That's encryption at rest.
That's DHCP.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes zero trust?

options.text: Never trust by default: verify every request, wherever it comes from
options.why: Zero trust checks identity, device and context for each request instead of trusting the internal network.
That's the old perimeter model zero trust replaces.
Zero trust allows remote access, but verifies it.
Shared passwords are the opposite of verifying each identity.

questions.stem: Which IPv6 range is link-local, like IPv4's 169.254 addresses?

options.why: Every IPv6 interface has an fe80:: link-local address that only works on the local link.
::1 is the IPv6 loopback address.
That's the global unicast range used on the internet.
That's multicast.

questions.stem: Which routing protocol is a link-state protocol commonly used inside a single organisation?

options.why: OSPF is a link-state interior gateway protocol: routers share link information and each works out the best paths.
BGP is the exterior protocol that connects organisations across the internet.
RIP is a distance-vector protocol that only counts hops.
NAT translates addresses; it isn't a routing protocol.

questions.stem: A router knows two routes to the same network: a static route and one learned by OSPF. Which does it normally use?

options.text: The static route, because it has a lower administrative distance
options.why: Administrative distance ranks how trustworthy a source is. Static routes default to 1, OSPF to 110, and lower wins.

options.text: The OSPF route, because dynamic routes always win
options.why: Dynamic routes don't automatically beat static ones; administrative distance decides.
More hops is never a reason to prefer a route.
Order doesn't matter; administrative distance, then metric, decide.

questions.stem: What does a VLAN do?

options.text: Splits one physical switch into separate logical networks, each its own broadcast domain
options.why: Devices in different VLANs can't talk directly; traffic between them must be routed.
VLANs are about separation, not speed.
VLAN tags aren't encryption.

options.text: Connects the network to the internet
options.why: That's the router's job.

questions.stem: Which standard adds a VLAN tag to frames on a trunk link between switches?

options.why: 802.1Q inserts a 4-byte tag with the VLAN ID so one link can carry many VLANs.
802.11 is Wi-Fi.
802.3af is Power over Ethernet.
802.1X is port-based network access control (authentication).

questions.stem: Why do switches run Spanning Tree Protocol?

options.text: To stop loops when there are redundant links between switches
options.why: Loops create broadcast storms. STP blocks redundant paths until they're needed.
That's DHCP.
STP doesn't encrypt anything.

options.text: To share traffic equally across all links
options.why: STP blocks redundant links rather than load-balancing across them.

questions.stem: Which Wi-Fi band reaches furthest but suffers the most interference from other devices?

options.why: Lower frequencies travel further and through walls better, but 2.4 GHz is crowded and shared with microwaves and Bluetooth.
5 GHz is faster with less interference, but shorter range.
6 GHz (Wi-Fi 6E/7) has the shortest range of the three.
60 GHz is very short-range, roughly within one room.

questions.stem: Which wireless security setting should a new office network use?

options.why: WPA3 is the current standard, with stronger protection against password guessing.
WEP was broken decades ago and can be cracked in minutes.
TKIP is deprecated and weak.

options.text: An open network with a hidden SSID
options.why: Hiding the name isn't security; the traffic is still unencrypted.

questions.stem: Why do 2.4 GHz networks use channels 1, 6 and 11?

options.text: They don't overlap, so neighbouring access points don't interfere
options.why: Other 2.4 GHz channels overlap. Using 1, 6 and 11 avoids co-channel and adjacent-channel interference.
Every channel has the same width; these just don't overlap.
Security settings don't depend on the channel.
Range doesn't depend on the channel number.

questions.stem: Why do data centres arrange racks into hot and cold aisles?

options.text: To keep cool intake air separate from hot exhaust air, so cooling works efficiently
options.why: Equipment pulls cool air from the cold aisle and blows hot air into the hot aisle, so the two don't mix.
Aisle layout is about airflow.
Fire suppression is a separate system.
Access control is handled separately.

questions.stem: What does a UPS provide?

options.text: Short-term battery power so equipment keeps running or shuts down cleanly
options.why: A UPS covers short outages and dips, long enough to shut down safely or for a generator to start.

options.text: Power for days during a long outage
options.why: That's a generator's job.
A UPS is about power, not connectivity.
Power protection doesn't change bandwidth.

questions.stem: Before changing a core switch's configuration, what should normally happen first?

options.text: It goes through change management: approval, a scheduled window and a rollback plan
options.why: Change management cuts the risk of outages and makes sure someone can undo the change.

options.text: Make the change, then tell people
options.why: Unannounced changes cause unexpected outages.
Rebooting every switch causes an outage and does nothing to make the change safer.
You want logs during a change, not fewer.

questions.stem: Which document shows how devices are physically and logically connected?

options.why: Physical and logical diagrams show devices, links, VLANs and addressing.
That sets rules for how people may use systems.
An SLA defines the service a provider promises.
An NDA is a confidentiality contract.

questions.stem: Which protocol lets a monitoring system poll devices for counters such as interface errors?

options.why: SNMP managers poll devices on UDP 161; devices can also send alerts (traps) on UDP 162.
Syslog is devices pushing log messages, not polling counters.
NTP synchronises time.
SMTP sends email.

questions.stem: Why record a baseline of normal network performance?

options.text: So you can spot when something becomes abnormal
options.why: Without knowing what normal looks like, you can't tell whether today's traffic is a problem.
A baseline is a measurement, not a tweak.
DHCP doesn't use baselines.
Baselines don't encrypt anything.

questions.stem: What does RPO (recovery point objective) describe?

options.text: How much data, measured in time, you can afford to lose
options.why: An RPO of 4 hours means backups must be at most 4 hours old.

options.text: How long systems can be down
options.why: That's the RTO (recovery time objective).
That's MTBF.
Cost isn't what RPO measures.

questions.stem: Which disaster recovery site can take over almost immediately?

options.why: A hot site has equipment running with current data, ready to switch over.
A warm site has equipment but needs data restored first, so it takes hours or days.
A cold site is space and power only, so recovery takes the longest.
Tapes protect data but provide no systems to run on.

questions.stem: Which DNS record maps a name to an IPv6 address?

options.why: AAAA ('quad A') records hold IPv6 addresses.
A records hold IPv4 addresses.
MX records name the mail servers for a domain.
A CNAME is an alias pointing to another name.

questions.stem: How can an IPv6 device give itself an address without a DHCP server?

options.why: Stateless address autoconfiguration builds an address from the prefix in the router's advertisements.
APIPA is IPv4's last-resort self-assigned address (169.254.x.x).
NAT translates addresses; it doesn't assign them.
ARP maps IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses.

questions.stem: Which service keeps device clocks in sync, so logs from different systems line up?

options.why: NTP (UDP 123) synchronises clocks. Accurate time matters for logs, certificates and authentication.
SNMP is for monitoring.
DNS resolves names.
LDAP is a directory service.

questions.stem: An admin plugs into a switch's console port because the network itself is down. What's this called?

options.why: Out-of-band management uses a separate path, such as a console port, so it works even when the network doesn't.
In-band management goes over the production network, which is down here.
That links two networks.
A jump box is a hardened server admins connect through.

questions.stem: What's a jump box (jump server) for?

options.text: A hardened single point admins connect through to reach sensitive systems
options.why: Funnelling admin access through one well-protected, logged host shrinks the attack surface.
Jump boxes are about controlled access, not speed.
A jump box controls administrator access; it doesn't answer DNS queries.
Public servers belong in a screened subnet, not on a jump box.

questions.stem: Which VPN type permanently connects two office networks?

options.why: Gateways at each office keep a tunnel up, so the two networks act as one.
Client-to-site connects one remote user.
Clientless VPN gives a user access through a web browser.
Split tunnelling describes which traffic goes through a VPN, not what it connects.

questions.stem: Comparing a file's hash before and after a download protects which part of the CIA triad?

options.why: A matching hash shows the file wasn't changed.
Confidentiality is about keeping data secret, for example with encryption.
Availability is about systems being up when needed.
That needs digital signatures tied to an identity, not just a hash, and it isn't part of the triad.

questions.stem: Which protocol commonly provides central authentication for 802.1X Wi-Fi and wired port access?

options.why: The switch or access point passes credentials to a RADIUS server, which approves or denies access.
TFTP is a simple file transfer protocol.
SNMP is for monitoring.
FTP transfers files.

questions.stem: An attacker floods a switch with fake MAC addresses until it starts sending frames out of every port. What is this?

options.why: Once the MAC table is full, the switch floods frames like a hub, letting the attacker see others' traffic. Port security limits it.
ARP spoofing sends fake ARP replies to redirect traffic through the attacker.
VLAN hopping reaches another VLAN through trunk tricks.
DNS poisoning plants false name-to-address answers.

questions.stem: Users on one floor suddenly get addresses from the wrong range and can't reach anything.

options.text: A rogue DHCP server is handing out leases
options.why: An unauthorised DHCP server answering first gives bad addresses or a malicious gateway. DHCP snooping blocks it.
MAC flooding affects switching, not address assignment.
That would only affect wireless users who joined the fake network.
A DDoS overwhelms services; it doesn't change users' addresses.

questions.scenario: Wired users on the third floor report the network stopped working after lunch. Their PCs show addresses in 10.99.0.0/24, but the company uses 192.168.20.0/24.

questions.stem: A fake Wi-Fi access point copies the name of a café's real network. What is it called?

options.why: An evil twin lures people to connect so the attacker can intercept their traffic.
That's about address assignment.
Bluejacking sends unsolicited Bluetooth messages.
War driving is searching an area for wireless networks.

questions.stem: Which switch feature limits which MAC addresses may use a port?

options.why: Port security can allow specific or a set number of MAC addresses, and shut the port down on a violation.
STP prevents loops.
Trunking carries several VLANs over one link.
QoS prioritises traffic.

questions.stem: Where should a public web server go so a compromise doesn't expose the internal network?

options.why: A screened subnet sits between the internet and the internal network, with firewall rules limiting what it can reach.
A compromised server there sits next to staff PCs.
That puts the most sensitive systems next to the most exposed one.
Guest networks are for visitors, not servers.

questions.stem: Router access control lists end with an implicit rule. What does it do?

options.why: The implicit deny means traffic that matches no permit line is dropped.
That would make the ACL pointless.
Logging must be configured; it isn't implied.
No protocol is allowed by default.

questions.stem: What's the first step of the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology?

options.why: First gather information, question users, find symptoms and what changed.

options.text: Establish a theory of probable cause
options.why: That's step two, after identifying the problem.
Fixing comes later, after testing a theory and planning.
Documentation is the last step.

questions.stem: You've just fixed a fault. What should you do before documenting it?

options.text: Verify full system functionality and add preventive measures if needed
options.why: Check that everything works, not just the original symptom, and stop it recurring. Then document.
Planning comes before you implement the fix.
That's part of identifying the problem at the start.
Escalation is for problems you can't solve yourself.

questions.stem: A port's link light is off and a cable tester reports an open on one pair. What's the likely cause?

options.text: A broken or badly terminated cable
options.why: An 'open' means a wire has no continuity. Re-terminate or replace the cable.
A duplex mismatch gives a link with errors and slow speed, not no link at all.
DHCP problems happen after the link is up.
A wrong VLAN still shows a link light.

questions.stem: An interface shows a steadily rising count of CRC errors. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: A damaged cable or electrical interference
options.why: CRC errors mean frames arrive corrupted, usually from physical problems such as bad cables, EMI or bad connectors.
DNS can't corrupt frames.
Leases don't affect frame integrity.
Congestion causes drops and delay, not CRC errors.

questions.stem: Which fault fits these symptoms best?

options.why: Reaching an IP but not names points to name resolution. Check the DNS server settings, and test with nslookup.
If the gateway were wrong, pinging an internet IP would fail too.
A cable fault would stop the ping as well.
The ping proves the switch is forwarding traffic.

questions.scenario: A user can ping 8.8.8.8 successfully, but no website opens by name.

questions.stem: Two PCs keep showing 'duplicate IP address' warnings. What's the likely cause?

options.text: A static address was set that's also inside the DHCP pool
options.why: When DHCP hands out an address someone set manually, two devices clash. Exclude static addresses from the pool or use reservations.
DNS failures don't cause address conflicts.
Cables don't cause duplicate addresses.
That stops ping, not address assignment.

questions.stem: Voice calls sound choppy because packets arrive at uneven intervals. What is this called?

options.why: Jitter is variation in delay. Real-time traffic needs it low; QoS and jitter buffers help.
Latency is the overall delay, even if it's constant.
Packet loss is packets that never arrive.
Throughput is how much data gets through per second.

questions.stem: Wi-Fi is slow only near the office kitchen. What's the most likely cause?

options.text: Interference on the 2.4 GHz band from the microwave
options.why: Microwave ovens operate around 2.4 GHz. Use 5 GHz or move the access point and channels.
DNS wouldn't depend on where you stand.
That's a wired problem.
That would break things everywhere, not just near the kitchen.

questions.stem: Which command shows each router hop on the way to a destination?

options.why: traceroute lists every hop and its delay, so you can see where traffic stops or slows.
ping tests reachability and round-trip time, not the path.
nslookup queries DNS.
arp -a lists the local IP-to-MAC cache.

questions.stem: Which tool checks which IP address a name resolves to?

options.why: Both query DNS directly and show the answer and which server gave it.
netstat shows connections and listening ports.
ipconfig shows the local IP settings.
tcpdump captures packets.

questions.stem: Which tools capture network packets so you can inspect them?

options.why: Packet capture shows exactly what's on the wire, such as DHCP, DNS and TCP handshakes.
ping sends test packets; it doesn't capture traffic.
nslookup only queries DNS.
route shows or edits the routing table.
